Why Great Hires Fail at Startups.
Oct 5
Written By
Michail Katkoff
When
Garry Hill
recruited for SpaceX, interviews ran on Saturdays and Sundays. Push back on a weekend slot and you never got the interview. The calendar was the test.
People want to join startups for the same reasons people found them: ownership, speed, equity, the chance to matter.
Most have never worked without the scaffolding of an established company. No recruiting team, no clear lane, no logo to borrow credibility from. That's why great hires fail at startups.
Talent is rarely the problem. Their talent was just built for a different environment.
Garry has recruited at PlayStation, Amazon, Blizzard and Reddit, and is now the only person doing his job across
Makers Fund
's 130-plus portfolio companies. More than 20,000 interviews in, his view of who fits comes down to a different question for each side of the table.
Employees should ask whether they want the job or the idea of it.
Employers should test what a candidate actually did, not where they did it.
Founders should ask whether the person who fits today will still fit two stages from now, and that includes themselves.

Will a great employee from one company succeed in another?
Garry's answer is yes, but only downhill. Someone who made it at SpaceX would likely do fine at Amazon or PlayStation. The reverse rarely holds. SpaceX selected for mission obsession and tolerance for stress, so anyone who survived it had already been tested. For Garry, the through-line is grit.
"At Blizzard, the people who looked best on paper did the worst. Principal-level engineers and designers from top schools and leading tech companies struggled because it took a long time to build trust with the team. This top talent was typically used for quick wins. They often didn't have the grit to build trust. So they burnt out and spun out after about a year from Blizzard."
— Garry Hill
His own Blizzard and Amazon stories from the podcast are about driven, pedigreed people who failed because the environment rejected them, and not because they lacked drive. Drive gets you in the door. Whether you stay depends on fit with how the company actually works.
Fitting in takes grit and humility.
So
the useful interview makes sure the candidate understands the job they're walking into
, and whether they actually did the work on their resume.
Regarding resumes, especially with big-tech hires, separate the work from the team. Ask which part of the work they owned, then back-channel the people who sat next to them.
Garry also named
two types who underestimate startups
. One is the visionary designer who forgets it's a business. The other is the strong engineer, allergic to anything businessy, who suddenly has to sort out the finance stack because nobody else will.
It's common to assume that startups are not for people with kids. Yet Garry pointed out that a family isn't automatically the dealbreaker people might assume. Parents can and do thrive at startups.
What breaks the parent hire is dishonesty about the hours, from either the candidate or the founder.
Hire slower, wider, and with a process
The two mistakes Garry sees most in hiring are going both too fast and too narrow. Too fast means seats get filled because the founder, who's doing 8 things at the same time, wanted someone to fill the seat yesterday. Too narrow means hiring for titles rather than the role.
Referrals are the trap
. Every startup fills its first thirty seats with "I know a guy." Garry doesn't say stop. He says build the process first: who interviews, what they ask, five steps maximum. Then run referrals through it like everyone else.
"A famous logo tells you nothing about how someone performs."
— Garry Hill
The counterargument is real.
Jordan Mazer
, head of talent at a16z, pushes for speed because slow processes lose candidates, as he explained
in our podcast
. In California, with at-will employment, a fast mis-hire is cheap to undo. In most of Europe, it isn't. Your labour law matters as much as your philosophy.
In the early phase, you want T-shaped people, deep in one area and willing to cover the tangents. Because you're likely a pivot or two away from what your company should be building. Post Series A, when you have product-market fit, touching everything becomes the bottleneck, process arrives, and the CEO has to let go without pulling work back. Later stage needs people comfortable not being in every meeting, which is exactly where the scrappiest early hires struggle.
So what happens to the people who got you there?
I think of them as rocket boosters.
They do the hardest part of the flight, then detach, ideally thanked publicly. That's why Garry advocates for T-shaped talent. They are most likely to survive each evolution stage of the company.

Founders that turn into mascots or demigods
In scaled companies, lingering co-founders can act like demigods. No process applies to them, and they drag the company back to how things used to be. Garry agreed, then named the worse version: the co-founder who has no ownership and does nothing. A talking head. A mascot who supposedly represents "the culture." Left for everyone to wonder what they even do.
For co-founder candidates, Garry gets an hour and spends it probing for resilience.
He asks for a story the person didn't choose: a lost job, a failed product. Do they own it cleanly, or blame the market, bad managers, no onboarding? Did they climb out, or did luck?
Then comes the move I'm stealing. Mid-interview, he asks who their mentor was. Then he asks them to spell the name. Or their lead on that feature, spelled out, because he's going to contact them.
A reference in real time.
